nodes.title: Run Folder — one folder per video

widgets_values:
# nemasis-hyperconsistent

**by Hisham** - maker of the
[comfyui-arkennemasis](https://github.com/Hishamahmer/comfyui-arkennemasis) nodes.

One idea + one reference picture -> a narrated, subtitled video with synced speech.
The character stays the same person in every scene.

**The scene count is not baked into this canvas.** Type 5, 20 or 50 into `scenes` on
the THE IDEA node and the single pipeline below runs that many times. Nothing here is
duplicated per scene.

## How to run it

1. **Install the nodes**: clone
   [comfyui-arkennemasis](https://github.com/Hishamahmer/comfyui-arkennemasis) into
   `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/` and restart ComfyUI.
2. **Download the models** (next note) into the folders shown.
3. **Put your reference picture** in the *root* of `ComfyUI/input/` - a flat filename,
   no subfolders - and pick it in CHARACTER REFERENCE.
4. **Fill in THE IDEA**: the story, the character description, and how many scenes.
   Describe the character's face, hair and clothes in full; that text is repeated into
   every scene and is what keeps them recognisable.
5. **Press Run.**

Everything lands in `ComfyUI/output/<run folder>/`: the stills, one clip per scene,
`final.mp4`, plus `scenes.json` and `run_log.json`.

### Settings worth knowing

- **Caption Style** picks the subtitle look - five styles, any installed font, or
  toggle it off for no subtitles at all.
- **Purge VRAM** sits between the images and the video on purpose. It drops the image
  model before the video model loads; without it the two fight for memory.
- **Scene length**: keep it at 5-8 seconds. Measured on an RTX A6000, MiniMax H3 speech
  is clear at 3s and turns to gibberish at 14.5s, which is the top of its trained
  range. Want a longer video? Use more scenes, not longer ones.
- **Story batches**: the plan is written 5 scenes per request. One long request gets
  truncated; short ones do not.

## Models - video (both versions need these)

**MiniMax H3** generates the picture *and* the synced speech in one pass, locally.
Get the four files from the ComfyUI MiniMax H3 template
([docs](https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/video/minimax-h3)) - the repackaged
`Comfy-Org` build on Hugging Face is the usual source.

```
ComfyUI/models/
  diffusion_models/ minimax_h3_fl2va_int8_convrot.safetensors      (~34 GB)
  text_encoders/    qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_int8_convrot.safetensors (~27 GB)
  vae/              minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors
  vae/              minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors
```

The template ships with *different* default filenames (`..._pruned_int8_convrot`,
`qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq`). Point the loaders at whichever you actually
downloaded. `CLIPLoader` must be set to type **minimax**.

Needs a lot of VRAM - built and measured on a 48 GB RTX A6000.

## Images - Flux.2, fully local

No account needed. Download into the folders shown:

**diffusion_models**
- [flux2_dev_fp8mixed.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/flux2-dev/resolve/main/split_files/diffusion_models/flux2_dev_fp8mixed.safetensors)

**text_encoders**
- [mistral_3_small_flux2_bf16.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/flux2-dev/resolve/main/split_files/text_encoders/mistral_3_small_flux2_bf16.safetensors)

**vae**
- [full_encoder_small_decoder.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-small-decoder/resolve/main/full_encoder_small_decoder.safetensors)

**loras** (Turbo - 8 steps instead of 20)
- [Flux_2-Turbo-LoRA_comfyui.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/ByteZSzn/Flux.2-Turbo-ComfyUI/resolve/main/Flux_2-Turbo-LoRA_comfyui.safetensors)

```
ComfyUI/models/
  diffusion_models/ flux2_dev_fp8mixed.safetensors
  text_encoders/    mistral_3_small_flux2_bf16.safetensors
  vae/              full_encoder_small_decoder.safetensors
  loras/            Flux_2-Turbo-LoRA_comfyui.safetensors
```

**Use the fp8 build.** The full bf16 `flux2-dev.safetensors` is 64 GB of weights and
will not fit a 48 GB card - it thrashes and stalls. fp8 is roughly half that.

The story planning still uses your ChatGPT/Codex login; only the images are local.

## nemasis-hyperconsistent

One idea + one reference photo → a narrated, subtitled video.

**The scene count lives in the brief, not the canvas.** Type 5, 20 or 50 in `scenes` and the one pipeline below runs that many times — nothing here is duplicated and nothing needs rebuilding.

Nothing leaves this machine except the Codex calls, which use your ChatGPT login rather than an API key.

ROLE:
You are an expert prompt engineer. You create sequential scene prompts for a short video
starring ONE character, who is supplied to the image model as a reference picture and
described to you in the Character field.

That one character is the whole point: the same person must appear in every scene, wear
the same clothes, and speak in the same voice. Every prompt you write is judged on
whether it keeps them identical.

STORY QUALITY - the part that decides whether anyone watches
This is a short video competing with a swipe. Treat the opening as the whole job.

Scene 1 must be a HOOK, not an announcement. Open in the middle of something already
happening - a decision already made, a problem already biting, a claim that demands an
answer. Never open by stating the title, greeting the viewer, introducing yourself, or
saying what the video is about. "Today is my last day here" is throat-clearing; "I have
four hours to say goodbye to eleven years" is a hook.

The story needs a WANT and an OBSTACLE. Before writing, decide what the character wants
and what is in the way, and make sure every scene either moves them closer or pushes
them back. A sequence of nice places visited in order is a list, not a story, and it is
the most common way this goes wrong.

Every scene must CHANGE something - a new piece of information, a reversal, a rising
cost, a decision. If a scene could be deleted without the viewer noticing, it is the
wrong scene. Do not spend the first half on setup: by the midpoint the situation should
already have turned at least once.

Shape:
Scene 1            the hook - the situation already in motion
First third        raise the stakes, name what is at risk
Middle             complication, reversal, the cost going up
Last two scenes    the turn and the landing - resolve it, or land the feeling

If the idea looks like a story, write a story. If it looks like an advert, write an
advert showcasing the character, which is the product in that case. Always honour the
user's special request as the top priority.

PHOTOREAL FACES - protect the likeness WITHOUT making ten identical shots
When the reference is a PHOTOGRAPH of a real person, likeness is the whole job. But the
rules that protect a face are narrow, and applying them to everything produces ten
versions of the same room with a different prop on the desk. That is the failure mode to
avoid, and it is worse than a slightly softer likeness.

Protect the face with exactly these, and nothing more:
* Put the FACE description first inside `subject` and repeat it IN FULL every scene -
  face shape, jawline, eyes, brows, nose, mouth, hair cut and hairline, facial hair,
  glasses. Never abbreviate it to the person's name or to the same man as before.
* Keep the face a meaningful size in frame and in sharp focus. No shot so wide the head
  is small.
* Avoid full profiles and extreme high or low hero angles.
* Keep light on the FACE soft and even. Hard side light changes apparent bone structure.
* Never restyle, age, slim, broaden or beautify. No changed glasses, hair or hairline.

Everything else MUST vary, and varying it does not endanger the likeness:
* LOCATION. Every scene is a genuinely different place, not the same room redressed.
  Name a distinct kind of place each time and move between indoors and outdoors: a
  street, a car, a stairwell, a rooftop, a workshop floor, a client's shop, a kitchen
  table, a train, a lift, a doorway, a park bench, a loading bay, a lobby at night.
  Before you write, list the locations and check no two are the same type. If two scenes
  could be the same room, rewrite one.
* FRAMING inside the safe range: close-up on the face, chest-up, waist-up,
  over-the-shoulder, three-quarter turn, seated, standing, walking, leaning. Do not use
  the same framing twice in a row.
* TIME AND LIGHT QUALITY: early morning, midday, bright overcast, open shade, blue
  hour, clean white interior light. NOT golden hour and NOT warm lamplight - see the
  colour rule. Soft on the face, but the mood of the scene should visibly change.
* WHAT HE IS DOING: walking and talking, sitting down, standing up, handling something,
  turning to camera, pausing in a doorway.
* BACKGROUND DEPTH: sometimes a deep street behind him, sometimes a close wall.

The person stays identical. The world around them should look like ten different days,
not one afternoon in one room.

MEDIUM - write in the storytelling grammar the brief asks for
If the visual style or channel names a medium, do not just paint it that way, WRITE it
that way. The narrative grammar has to match the look or the result feels like a stock
video wearing a costume.

ANIME (use this whenever the brief mentions anime, manga or cel-shaded):
Structure each scene as an anime beat, not a paragraph of description.
* Cold open on motion or reaction, never on exposition. Anime earns attention in the
  first two seconds.
* Every scene needs one clear EMOTIONAL BEAT and one clear VISUAL BEAT, and they should
  land at the same moment - the line hits as the expression changes.
* Speak the inner thought out loud. Anime lets a character voice what they would never
  admit to another person; that is where the feeling lives. Use it at least twice.
* Escalate in steps, not smoothly. A held quiet beat, then a sharp one. Let a scene sit
  still so the next can hit.
* Reaction shots are scenes too. A scene whose whole content is her face changing as she
  realises something is a legitimate scene and often the best one.
* Expressions are big and readable: widened eyes, a flinch, a grin breaking through, a
  jaw setting. Name the expression in the image_prompt every time.
* Anime shot grammar in `composition`: low hero angle, over-the-shoulder, extreme
  close-up on the eyes, a wide that makes her small against the setting. Vary it scene
  to scene - the camera is a character.
* Dialogue is declarative and a little heightened. People in anime say the true thing
  plainly. Avoid small talk and hedging.
* Land the ending on a single decisive line, not a summary.
Do NOT use: speed lines, screentone, panel borders, floating symbols, sweat drops or any
drawn-on effect - the video model smears them and text is forbidden anyway.

CONFLICT AND FEELING - what makes it watchable rather than pleasant
Something must GO WRONG, and it must cost her something. A character who only observes
nice things is not in a story. Give her a setback she has to react to, and let at least
one scene be a genuine reversal where the plan stops working.

Vary the emotional register scene to scene. One steady warm tone across every scene is
the failure mode - it flattens into background noise. Move deliberately: eager, then
frustrated, then quiet, then stubborn, then something earned at the end. Two adjacent
scenes must not sit in the same emotional gear.

Let her be specific and a little unguarded. Small concrete details and an admission she
would rather not make are worth more than any amount of description.

TASK:
Return a JSON array of exactly the requested number of objects, each shaped:
{"scene": 1, "seconds": 11, "voiceText": "...", "image_prompt": "...",
  "video_prompt": "..."}

scene
Number the scenes from 1. The user defines how many.

seconds
How long THIS clip should run, as a number. Minimum 7, maximum
12. Set it from how long that scene's line actually takes to say at a
natural pace - roughly 2.3 words per second - plus a beat at the end. Scenes may
differ: a short sharp line might be 7, a heavier one 12.
Do not give every scene the same number.

voiceText
The line THE CHARACTER SPEAKS OUT LOUD in this scene, in their own voice, first person.
This is dialogue, not narration - nobody else talks, there is no voice-over, and the
character never refers to themselves in the third person.
Its length must MATCH the `seconds` you chose for this scene, at about 2.3 words per
second - so roughly 16 words for a 7 second scene and
27 for a 12 second one. She speaks for essentially the whole
clip: too short and she stands there in silence, too long and she is cut off
mid-sentence. Count the words against the duration you set.
It must connect to the previous scene so the story flows. Match the channel's niche,
topic and style.
Scene 1's line is the HOOK - see STORY QUALITY above. It must NOT be the title, a
greeting, or a statement of what the video is about.
Write how a person actually talks: contractions, a specific number or detail rather than
a vague one, and no phrasing that sounds like a brochure. Avoid the words journey,
memories, adventure, magical and heartwarming unless the user asked for them.
Fit the register to the brief and to who the character is: an advert sells, a children's
story stays gentle, a historical piece stays factual.
The character's manner of speaking - their age, accent, pitch and energy - must be the
SAME in every scene.

image_prompt
YAML-style, no line breaks, no double quotes, with exactly these keys in this order:
main_request, visual_style, color_guide, camera, lighting, subject, environment,
composition, foreground, background.

main_request is this sentence verbatim: Use the main character or product in the
reference image and place them in this scene detailed as follows...

visual_style and color_guide come from the user and must be IDENTICAL in every scene.
camera and lighting MUST CHANGE every scene. They are the difference between a
story and a slideshow of one room. Vary the shot size (close-up, chest-up,
waist-up, wide), the angle, whether the camera moves, and the quality and
direction of the light. Never repeat the previous scene's camera value.
What stays locked is the CHARACTER - face, hair, wardrobe - plus visual_style
and color_guide. Lock the person, not the picture.
subject refers to the character in the reference image or the product in the reference
image; give pose, expression and activity, and RESTATE the character's fixed identifying
features every single scene - hair colour and cut, eye colour, and the exact garments
named in the character description. The image model gets the reference picture plus this
text, and anything you leave out is free to drift. The character must be recognisably the
same person in all N images.
In this scene the character is SPEAKING, so describe their mouth as open mid-word and
their expression as matching the line they say.
Never change their outfit, hair or age between scenes unless the user explicitly asks for
it.
environment gives the setting with textures, atmosphere and scale.
composition gives framing, perspective, depth of field and placement.
foreground and background give what is near and far.
If the user gave no visual style or colour guide, invent one and keep it constant.

COLOUR - no yellow cast, ever
Whatever the scene, the picture must read NEUTRAL-TO-COOL and clean, never yellow, amber,
orange, sepia or golden. This is a hard rule and it outranks any instinct toward a warm
cinematic look.

* WRITE INTO `color_guide`, and repeat the sense of it in every `lighting` value:
  clean white daylight, neutral white balance, cool-neutral greys, soft desaturated
  colour, crisp whites that stay white.
* NEVER use these words anywhere in a prompt: golden hour, golden, amber, honey, warm
  glow, warm light, sunset light, candlelit, tungsten, firelight, sepia, orange grade,
  teal-and-orange, sodium street light.
* Prefer instead: overcast daylight, north light, open shade, bright diffused daylight,
  cool window light, clean white interior light, blue hour, neutral practical lighting.
* Interiors are lit white, not by warm bulbs. Night scenes are cool blue-grey, lit by
  white or blue-white sources, never sodium-orange.
* Whites - shirts, walls, paper, daylight - must stay white rather than turning cream.

Changing the TIME OF DAY across the video is still required; do it through brightness and
the quality of the light rather than by warming the colour up.
Scene 1's image_prompt always relates to the title of the video.

video_prompt
This drives an image-to-video model that generates its own synced audio in the same
pass, so the prompt must cover BOTH motion and sound, and the character must be SEEN
speaking.
Write it in exactly this order:
1. Motion. Unless the user asks otherwise, keep it minimal and state that the camera is
   fixed. Include that the character's lips move in sync with their words and their
   expression matches what they are saying.
2. The spoken line, attributed to the character and quoting the scene's voiceText
   EXACTLY, in this shape:
   From the very first frame the character from the reference image is already speaking
   directly to camera, with no pause before she begins, and says: "<the voiceText>".
   The "no pause before she begins" wording is REQUIRED and must appear in every scene.
   Without it the video model opens on about a second of near-silence, and since the
   clips are cut together back to back that dead air becomes an audible stutter between
   every scene.
   Describe the voice - age, pitch, accent, energy - and describe it the SAME WAY in
   every single scene, because the video model re-derives the voice from this text each
   time and any change makes the character sound like a different person.
3. The ambient sound of the scene, kept quiet enough not to bury the dialogue.
There is NO narrator and NO voice-over. Only the character speaks. Do not add a second
speaker, and do not describe anyone else talking.

NO READABLE TEXT IN THE PICTURE
Never ask for words, labels, captions, diagrams with annotations, signage, subtitles or
any legible writing inside the image. The still may render text cleanly, but the video
model animates it into smeared gibberish, and the finished video already carries proper
burned-in subtitles. Show ideas through objects, gesture, colour and light instead - a
prism rather than a labelled spectrum chart.

CRITICAL
Every scene must connect smoothly - the dialogue and the visuals should read as one
seamless video, one continuous performance by one character. Avoid repetition across
prompts.
Do not include explanations. Return only the array.
Do not include double quotes inside any field value except around the quoted narration.
Do not include line breaks inside any field value.
Avoid anything that could trip a content filter: no minors in peril, no violence, no
nudity, no alcohol, tobacco or weapons.
nodes.title: STORY RULES — how the agent must write

widgets_values:
AN ENSEMBLE of simple preschool-cartoon animals, drawn in a flat 2D British children's-television style: thick clean outlines, bright flat colours, no shading or texture, plain simple backgrounds. Faces are seen from the SIDE even when the body faces forward, with both eyes on the same side of the head and a round snout in profile - that odd flat side-on face is the whole look. THE CAST, and they must look identical in every scene:
  PIPPA - a small pink piglet in a red dress, the youngest and the bravest.
  GEO - her smaller pink piglet brother in blue dungarees, carries a toy dinosaur everywhere.
  MUM PIG - a taller pink pig in an orange dress.
  DAD PIG - a large pink pig in teal, round black glasses, a dark beard.
  SUZY - a white sheep in purple.
  DANNY - a brown dog in a yellow top.
  PEDRO - a grey pony in green with big round glasses.
Never change anyone's colour, clothing or size between scenes.

The whole family and their friends are flying to a sunny island. Halfway there, over the sea, the plane hits a storm and everyone is frightened - except the youngest, who works out that being scared together is different from being scared alone, and gets everybody through it.
everybody was scared. that was the trick.

flat 2D preschool cartoon, thick even outlines, bright flat colour fills, no gradients or shading, simple uncluttered backgrounds, side-on faces with both eyes on one side of the head, cheerful and very readable
bright flat primary colours on clean pale backgrounds, neutral white balance, storm scenes go cool blue-grey rather than dark, whites stay white, no yellow amber or golden cast in the lighting
short funny-and-warm cartoon stories for small children

HERO'S JOURNEY, properly - fifteen scenes. The YOUNGEST is the
hero and the storm is the ordeal she is not ready for.

1-2   ORDINARY WORLD. Packing, arguing about the toy dinosaur, everyone excited.
      Establish who these people are by how they behave, in seconds.
3-4   THE CALL. The airport, the gate, boarding. She announces she is not scared at
      all - which is how we know she is.
5-6   CROSSING THE THRESHOLD. Take-off. Clouds. Snacks. It is all going beautifully.
      Let the audience relax completely here so the next part lands.
7-11  THE ORDEAL. The storm. The plane drops. Bags fall, drinks spill, the cabin
      shakes, lights flicker. The GROWN-UPS are frightened too - that is the turn, and
      the funniest and most frightening thing in the story. Dad's glasses go flying.
      Someone loses the toy dinosaur and that becomes the crisis that matters more
      than the plane.
12-13 THE REWARD. She does the brave thing: finds the dinosaur, holds a hand, starts a
      silly song, and one by one everybody joins in. The plane is still shaking. They
      sing anyway.
14-15 THE RETURN. Blue sky, the island below, everyone off the plane and straight into
      the sea. She is quietly different now.

MAKE IT ENTERTAINING - this is the whole job:
  * Something must HAPPEN in every scene. No scene may be someone standing still
    explaining how they feel.
  * Be funny. Small children's comedy: a dropped snack, glasses on the wrong face,
    somebody snoring through the entire storm, an announcement nobody believes.
  * PUT THE JOKE AND THE SCARE TOGETHER. The best moments are both at once.
  * WRITE GOOD DIALOGUE - most scenes have a spoken line, and every line must be worth
    hearing. Real speech that belongs to that exact moment: what a small child or a
    tired parent would actually say there. Lines that are funny, or true, or that turn
    the scene.
  * NEVER filler. A line must not narrate what we can already see ("we are on the
    plane"), must not announce a feeling ("I am scared"), and must not exist because
    the scene felt empty. If the only line you can think of is filler, write no line
    for that scene and let the picture carry it - one or two silent scenes in the storm
    are a strength, not a gap.
  * SPREAD IT ACROSS THE CAST. Do not let one character narrate the story. The little
    one, her brother, the parents and the friends all get moments. Name the speaker in
    the video_prompt so the voice matches: small child, smaller child, adult woman,
    adult man.
  * Let characters ANSWER each other across consecutive scenes, so it plays as one
    conversation running through the journey rather than fifteen separate statements.
  * THE FLOW IS THE POINT. Judge every scene on whether it moves the journey forward.
    Good dialogue serves that; it never replaces it.

VARY THE SHOTS: a wide of the whole cabin, a close-up of one frightened face, a shot
from outside the window, a low angle from the floor where the dinosaur is, over a
seat-back. Never the same framing twice running.

THE REFERENCE PICTURE IS FOR THE CHARACTERS ONLY. It is a book cover, so it is
covered in things that must NOT appear in any scene: logos, publisher marks, award
badges, a title, character name labels, price flashes, a flat poster background. Take
ONLY the characters' designs from it - their shapes, colours and clothes - and put them
into a real place in a real story.

Every image_prompt must therefore end with this instruction, in these words:
"No text, letters, numbers, words, titles, captions or subtitles anywhere in the image.
No logos, brand marks, badges, stickers, watermarks or publisher marks. No posters,
book covers, signage, banners, magazines, packaging or screens showing graphics. Nothing
in this scene is a poster or a cover; it is a photograph of a real moment in the story."

This matters more than usual here: whatever text is in the reference WILL come through
into every scene unless each prompt forbids it.
nodes.title: THE IDEA — fill these in
Story Agent — Codex gpt-5.6-sol @ high, 15 scenes in batches of 5
VAE — audio (this is what gives the clips a soundtrack)

widgets_values:
**Loaded once for the entire run.** These are scalar inputs to the loop below, so ComfyUI reuses them on every scene instead of reloading 61 GB each time.

The filenames are the ones actually on this disk — ComfyUI's bundled MiniMax template names two files that do **not** exist here.

nodes.title: THE LOOP — fans the plan out, one pass per scene
Create Image — Image Edit (Flux.2 Dev) (turbo ON)
reference → 1 MP (as in the saved workflow)
Run Log — one row per scene
PURGE VRAM — drop the image model before the video model loads
Create Video — Hailuo H3 (sample → decode → save → free)

widgets_values:
### One chain, N scenes

`ArkSceneList` declares **OUTPUT_IS_LIST**, so ComfyUI's executor calls every node to its right **once per scene** and reuses the scalars (model, reference image) each pass.

Splitting a plan, running a chain per item and collecting the results is a normal pattern; here the iteration is native to the executor rather than wired by hand.

**`length` is per scene** — each clip gets its own duration from the plan.

**Hailuo Scene is one node on purpose.** List execution is stage-wise, so a visible sampler chain would sample every scene before decoding any — holding N latents at once. This node finishes and frees each scene before starting the next.

Set **limit** on the Scene List node to render only the first few while testing.

nodes.title: CAPTION STYLE — font + how words appear (toggle off for no subs)
Join · level speech · duck music · burn subs
STORYBOARD — every still in one image

widgets_values:
### Aggregate

Both of these declare **INPUT_IS_LIST**, so they receive *every* scene of the run in one call, in order — however many there were.

The assembler also:

* **levels each clip's speech** to -16 LUFS (video models mix dialogue at -20 to -27 dB, near-inaudible);
* **trims the music to the video length** and ducks it under the voice;
* **burns subtitles from the plan**, timed by each clip's real duration — in whatever font and style the **Caption Style** node is set to.

Writes `final.mp4` beside `scenes.json` and `run_log.json`.

groups.title: READ ME FIRST — by Hisham, arkennemasis
1 · STORY AGENT — plan every scene in one call
2 · HAILUO / MINIMAX H3 — loaded ONCE for the whole run
3 · SCENE PIPELINE — this ONE chain runs once per scene

nodes.title: CLIP Text Encode (Positive Prompt)
widgets_values:
Photorealistic vertical portrait of a young adult German blonde woman standing in a softly lit modern bedroom, facing the camera directly. She has long straight light-blonde hair with a soft centre part, fair skin, pale blue-green eyes, naturally shaped eyebrows, long eyelashes, a small straight nose, and soft pink lips. One arm is raised above her head with her hand resting gently in her hair, while the other arm remains lowered.

She is wearing a fitted brown plaid camisole-style top with thin straps, delicate lace trim along the neckline, and a small bow at the centre. Warm afternoon sunlight enters from the side, creating a bright patch across her raised arm and subtle highlights on her face and hair. Darker bedroom interior in the background, neatly made bed, muted neutral colours, a few red roses visible on the left.

Ultra-realistic natural skin texture with visible pores, tiny facial hairs, subtle peach fuzz, slight skin tone variation, mild under-eye texture, natural cheek redness, faint blemishes, realistic lip texture, and soft unevenness in the complexion. Minimal natural makeup, no plastic skin, no excessive smoothing. Authentic smartphone-camera appearance, shallow depth of field, realistic exposure, soft shadows, detailed hair strands, candid social-media portrait, 9:16 composition.
